description: FSA temperature controls, date marks, personal hygiene and cross-contamination prevention.
content_html:
Temperature: The Most Important Food Safety Control

If you could only remember one food safety principle, it would be this: temperature controls bacterial growth. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) publishes specific temperature guidelines that underpin every aspect of safe food handling, and the written paper tests exact figures. Vague answers like “keep it cold” or “cook it until hot” will not earn marks. Memorise these numbers.

Key Fact

FSA temperature guidelines: Freezing: –18°C — bacteria cannot multiply. Chilling: 0 to below 5°C — bacterial growth is very slow. Danger zone: 5 to 63°C — bacteria multiply rapidly. Cooking and reheating: 75°C — most harmful bacteria are destroyed.

The temperature danger zone is the range 5°C to 63°C. This is why food should never be left at room temperature (typically 18–22°C, well inside the danger zone) for longer than necessary. Bacteria can double in number every 20 minutes at room temperature — a portion of cooked rice left on a worktop for two hours can contain many millions more bacteria than one put straight into the fridge.

Buying and Storing Food Safely

Safe food handling begins at the point of purchase, not when you get home. When shopping, always:

  • Check date marks before buying. ‘Use by’ dates apply to high-risk foods such as raw meat, cooked meat products and soft cheeses — consuming after this date could harm health. ‘Best before’ dates apply to lower-risk foods such as tinned goods, dried pasta and frozen peas; the food remains safe after this date but may decline in quality.
  • Pack raw meat and fish in separate bags from ready-to-eat foods to prevent drip contamination.
  • Choose chilled and frozen foods last in a supermarket shop and transport them in insulated bags to minimise the time spent in the danger zone.

‘Use by’ is a food safety date. Eating food after its use-by date is a genuine health risk, regardless of whether it looks or smells fine — harmful bacteria do not always cause visible or olfactory changes. ‘Best before’ is a quality date. After a ‘best before’ date, the food may be less flavoursome, have a different texture or lose some nutritional value, but it is not automatically unsafe. A can of tomatoes three days past its best-before date is still safe to eat; a pack of cooked prawns one day past its use-by date should be discarded. In an exam, be precise: low-risk ambient foods carry ‘best before’ labels; high-risk perishable foods carry ‘use by’ labels.

At home, correct use of domestic refrigerators and freezers is essential:

  • Fridges should run at 0 to below 5°C. Many domestic fridges are set too warm; an internal thermometer is a good investment.
  • Raw meat and fish should be stored on the bottom shelf of the fridge in sealed containers to prevent drip onto cooked or ready-to-eat foods below.
  • Freezers should run at –18°C. Food is safe indefinitely in a correctly operating freezer, although quality declines over time.
  • Ambient foods — dry goods such as flour, rice, tinned goods, pasta and breakfast cereals — should be stored in sealed containers in cool, dry, ventilated cupboards away from direct sunlight and damp. Ambient storage prevents moisture absorption (which could allow mould and bacterial growth) and pest contamination.
  • All open or partially used foods should be covered. Covering prevents contamination from airborne bacteria, insects and dust, and reduces moisture loss from chilled foods.
Key Fact

Raw meat and fish must be stored on the bottom shelf of the fridge in sealed containers to prevent bacterial cross-contamination from drips onto ready-to-eat foods. The fridge must run at 0 to below 5°C — not at room temperature or “just cold enough”.

Personal Hygiene and Preventing Cross-Contamination

Cross-contamination is the most common route by which bacteria from raw food reach ready-to-eat food. Safe food preparation requires vigilance at every stage:

  • Personal hygiene: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds before handling food, after handling raw meat or fish, after visiting the toilet, after touching the face or hair, after handling waste, and after touching pets. Cover cuts and wounds with blue waterproof plasters (blue so that if they fall into food, they are visible).
  • Clean work surfaces: Wipe surfaces with antibacterial cleaner between tasks. A damp cloth is not sufficient — it spreads bacteria. Use paper towels or a freshly laundered cloth.
  • Separate raw and cooked foods: Use separate chopping boards and knives for raw meat/fish and for ready-to-eat foods. Colour-coded systems (e.g. red boards for raw meat, green for vegetables, yellow for cooked meat) reduce the risk of confusing equipment.
  • Defrosting: Defrost frozen foods thoroughly in the fridge, not at room temperature. Defrosting at room temperature means the outer layers of the food spend time in the danger zone while the centre is still frozen. Large items such as a frozen chicken need 24 hours in the fridge per kilogram. Cook food promptly after defrosting; do not refreeze unless it has been cooked first.

Cooking food to 75°C throughout destroys most harmful bacteria, including campylobacter and salmonella. The critical word is “throughout” — the surface of a chicken breast may be 75°C while the thickest part near the bone is still below 60°C. A food temperature probe inserted into the thickest part of the meat is the only reliable way to check that the correct temperature has been reached. Visual checks (looking for clear juices, no pink meat) can be used alongside a probe but are not sufficient alone, especially for large poultry pieces or rolled joints. After use, the probe must be cleaned and sanitised before being used on another food to avoid cross-contamination.

When reheating food, it must also reach 75°C throughout. Food should only be reheated once — multiple reheat cycles increase the time food spends in the danger zone and raise the risk of bacterial growth. Rice is a particular concern: cooked rice that has been cooled quickly and refrigerated within two hours can be reheated safely once; rice that has been left at room temperature is a high-risk food because of the risk of Bacillus cereus toxins (though this specific bacterium is not on the specification, the principle of prompt cooling and reheating applies to all cooked grains and protein-rich foods).

High-risk foods — cooked poultry, egg dishes, shellfish, soft cheeses and cooked rice — require particular attention throughout the buy, store, prepare, cook and serve chain. Every stage at which these foods could enter the temperature danger zone or be exposed to raw food represents a contamination risk that must be actively managed.
exam_tip_html: Temperature questions are some of the most reliably marked items on the written paper because there are exact correct answers. A common mistake is writing “keep food cold” or “below freezing” when a mark scheme requires a specific number. Learn the FSA figures by heart: freezing –18°C, chilling 0 to below 5°C, danger zone 5 to 63°C, cooking and reheating 75°C. For a ‘use by’ vs ‘best before’ question, the key distinction is safety vs quality — state this clearly and support it with an example of each. On a 12-mark Evaluate question about food safety practice, top-band answers do not simply list rules: they apply the rules to the specific scenario, explain the consequences of failing each control (e.g. “if raw chicken drips onto the salad below, campylobacter is transferred to a food that will not be cooked, so the bacteria will not be destroyed before eating”), weigh which controls are most critical in the given context, and reach a supported judgement. The judgement must be explicit — do not end by listing; end by saying which factor poses the greatest risk and why.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exact FSA temperatures are non-negotiable: freezing –18°C, chilling 0 to below 5°C, danger zone 5–63°C, cooking and reheating 75°C. Approximate answers lose marks.
  • ‘Use by’ is a food safety date; ‘best before’ is a quality date — only use-by dates carry a genuine health risk if exceeded.
  • Cross-contamination from raw to ready-to-eat foods via hands, surfaces and equipment is the most common preparation risk; colour-coded boards, thorough hand washing and a food temperature probe are the key controls.

practice_questions.text:
What is the correct temperature for a domestic freezer, according to Food Standards Agency guidelines?
A. 0°C
B. −5°C
C. −18°C
D. −25°C
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C (−18°C). 0°C is the lower limit for chilling, not freezing. −5°C and −25°C are not the FSA-specified freezer temperature.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a 'use by' date and a 'best before' date on food packaging.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct statement, up to 2 marks. 'Use by' — a food safety date; eating after this date poses a health risk; applies to perishable high-risk foods. 'Best before' — a quality date; food may decline in flavour, texture or nutritional value after this date but is not necessarily unsafe; applies to lower-risk ambient foods such as tinned goods or dried pasta. Both distinctions must be present for both marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe three personal hygiene practices a food handler should follow when preparing a chicken stir-fry.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly described practice, up to 3 marks. Accept: wash hands thoroughly with soap and warm water before handling food; wash hands after handling raw chicken before touching other ingredients; cover any cuts with a blue waterproof plaster; tie back hair/wear a hair covering; avoid touching the face, nose or mouth during preparation; wear clean clothing. Answers must describe the practice, not just state a vague rule.

practice_questions.text: Theo is a trainee chef who cooks a whole roast chicken. The skin looks golden and the juices run clear, but when he inserts a temperature probe into the thickest part of the breast, the reading shows 68°C. Explain the action Theo should take and why it is necessary.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct action (return the chicken to the oven / continue cooking); 1 mark for explanation of why (the internal temperature has not yet reached 75°C, so harmful bacteria — such as campylobacter or salmonella — may not have been destroyed); 1 mark for explaining why visual checks alone are insufficient (surface appearance can look cooked while the centre remains below 75°C); 1 mark for reference to the role of the probe (the probe measures internal temperature, which is the only reliable indicator of safety). Must use linking language for the explanation marks.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effectively a home cook could manage the food safety risks when preparing, cooking and serving a buffet of cooked chicken, egg mayonnaise and prawn cocktail for a family celebration.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Comprehensive coverage of buying and storage risks (temperature control, raw-cooked separation, correct fridge shelf placement), preparation risks (cross-contamination from raw poultry via hands and equipment; campylobacter and salmonella; colour-coded boards; handwashing), cooking risks (chicken must reach 75°C throughout; use of a temperature probe; not relying on visual checks alone), and serving/holding risks (all three dishes — chicken, egg mayo and prawn cocktail — are high-risk chilled foods that must stay below 5°C on the buffet; time in danger zone; staphylococcus aureus risk from food handlers). Evaluates the feasibility of home cooks managing all risks consistently (lacks commercial equipment, training, probes; emotional distraction at a celebration). Reaches a supported judgement with weighing — e.g. which risk factor is hardest to control in a domestic setting and why. Uses accurate technical vocabulary throughout.

Secure (7–9 marks): Most stages addressed; at least three bacteria or contamination routes named with correct controls; some evaluation of difficulty/effectiveness rather than just listing rules; judgement present but may not be fully supported.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant safety points listed but mostly as rules without evaluation; one or two bacteria named; controls given; little or no assessment of how effectively a home cook could manage all risks; no clear judgement or judgement unsupported.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic rules listed (cook thoroughly, wash hands, keep food cold) with little or no bacterial knowledge, no evaluation, and no judgement.

practice_questions.text: Give the temperature of the food temperature danger zone.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the lower boundary (5°C); 1 mark for the upper boundary (63°C). Both must be correct and must be stated as a range (e.g. '5°C to 63°C') for 2 marks. Accepting each boundary independently: 1 mark for 5°C alone; 1 mark for 63°C alone. Vague answers such as 'room temperature' or 'between cold and hot' score 0.

knowledge_checks.q: At what temperature should a domestic fridge operate to keep food safe?
Which type of date mark indicates that eating the food after this date poses a genuine health risk?
Bacteria multiply most rapidly between 5°C and 63°C — a range known as the temperature _____ zone.
To prevent cross-contamination, raw meat should be stored on the _____ shelf of the fridge.
Match each food safety temperature to its purpose.
right: Cooking and reheating — most bacteria destroyed

flashcard_questions.q: What is the FSA recommended freezer temperature?
What temperature range is the food safety danger zone?
To what internal temperature must food be cooked to destroy most harmful bacteria?
What temperature should a domestic fridge run at?
What is the food temperature danger zone?
flashcard_questions.a: 5°C to 63°C — the range where most harmful bacteria multiply most rapidly.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a 'use by' date and a 'best before' date?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Use by' is a safety date; 'best before' is a quality date.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must raw meat be stored on the bottom shelf of the fridge?
flashcard_questions.a: To prevent bacteria from dripping onto ready-to-eat foods on lower shelves.
The transfer of harmful bacteria from raw food to ready-to-eat food via hands, surfaces or equipment.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should frozen food be defrosted in the fridge rather than at room temperature?
flashcard_questions.a: Room temperature is in the danger zone; fridge defrosting keeps bacteria growth very slow.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a food temperature probe used for?
flashcard_questions.a: To measure the internal temperature of food and confirm it has reached 75°C throughout.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are blue waterproof plasters used to cover cuts in food preparation?
flashcard_questions.a: Blue is visible if the plaster falls into food, allowing contaminated food to be identified.

flashcard_questions.q: How many times should cooked food be reheated?
flashcard_questions.a: Only once — multiple reheat cycles increase time in the danger zone.

glossary_terms.definition: The temperature range of 5°C to 63°C within which most harmful bacteria multiply most rapidly in food.
Labels on packaged food showing the date after which the food must not be eaten (use-by) or the date before which the food is at its best quality (best before).
The transfer of harmful bacteria from one food (usually raw) to another (usually cooked or ready-to-eat) via hands, surfaces or equipment.
A probe inserted into the thickest part of food to measure its internal temperature and confirm it has reached a safe cooking temperature.
